newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ easing seen later than sooner after wages data.
newsitem.headline: NZ easing seen later than sooner after wages data.

text.p: Workers may like higher wages shown in the latest data but the higher-than-expected rates will force the Reserve Bank to defer an easing of monetary policy until as late as possible, economists said on Tuesday.
"It's very positive if you received the wages but not that positive if you are looking for an imminent easing in monetary policy," said National Bank chief economist Adrian Orr.

"I think the Reserve Bank will take more comfort than it has done in the level of the exchange rate just at the moment and will certainly hold out until its December statement before having to say anything," he said.
Statistisics New Zealand said that average hourly earnings rose 3.3 percent in the May year with private sector earnings rising 4.0 percent, including a 1.5 percent rise in the May quarter.
"This is a surprise on the upside," Bank of New Zealand chief economist Tony Alexander said.
BNZ was expecting a private sector wages to rise 1.2 percent in the quarter.
"There is certainly strong evidence of the economy slowing but it is not feeding through into rate of wages," he said.
Employment growth would be weaker in future as firms found they could not afford to take on more workers and there would be pressure to pass on higher wage costs via higher prices."

"I think it is going to make the Reserve Bank more cautious about easing. It certainly pushes it well out to very late this year or the March quarter next year before they send any explicit signal," Alexander said.
"That doesn't necessarily mean that you are not going to get a market-driven easing anyway, not necessarily by the bills but by the bonds."
He said the long-end of the yield curve had already begun to ease as 10-year bond yields fell and that was translating into the retail sector through lower fixed interest mortgage rates.
The Reserve Bank said in its September economic projections it would ease monetary conditions in due course provided there was clear evidence of a easing in inflation pressure.
ANZ Bank chief economist Paul Stewart said the data was stronger than he had expected and the risk of inflation from higher wages would clearly concern the Reserve Bank.

Asked if inflation had peaked, he said: "There's certainly no confirmation of that. The argument that the Reserve Bank were running in the (September) economic projections is that wage pressures would peak in the June quarter and then moderate.
"Now that may be the case, but even if it is, we suspect that that four percent (private sector) figure is higher than what they would have been anticipating."

"I think it just reinforces the risks to the inflation outlook and the fact that although some easing in monetary policy is clearly anticipated over the next 12 months, that we can't be assured of that at this point in time."

Economists said the New Zealand dollar and high short-term interest rates would be underpinned by today's data. The 90-day bank bills rose two basis points to 9.85 percent after the release of the data.
